name: Comedone extractor
description: Double-ended steel instrument with perforated cups used to press out comedone contents.
parts: Two hemispherical cups, one at each end
Central perforation in each cup with blunt margins
Sinuous (S-curved) shape for better handling and localised pressure
uses: Expression of open and closed comedones in acne
Expression of contents of nevus comedonicus and senile (solar) comedones
how_to_hold: Held at the central handle like a pen; cup kept perpendicular to the skin.
method: Place the cup perforation over the plugged follicular opening of an open comedone
Apply gentle, firm pressure perpendicularly downward
Comedone contents extrude through the hole and collect in the cup
For closed comedones first nick the surface with a sterile lancet or needle, then express the same way
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Pressure must be perpendicular, not sliding, to avoid trauma and scarring
Closed comedones need an artificial opening first

name: Molluscum curette
description: Double-ended curette with a small round or oval cutting loop, used to scoop out superficial lesions.
parts: Round or oval loop with cutting edge at either end
types: Loop sizes 1-10 mm; 3-4 mm most commonly used
uses: Extraction of molluscum contagiosum
Curettage of seborrheic keratosis, stucco keratosis, verruca plana and actinic keratosis
how_to_hold: Pencil (fountain-pen) grip between thumb, index and middle finger, or potato-peeler grip with the handle in the distal interdigital fold of the index finger and thumb as a stable base; stretch the skin with the other hand.
method: Stretch the skin around the lesion with the other hand
Engage the lesion edge with the loop
Scoop out with a single firm stroke, keeping the curette at an angle to the skin
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Two holding techniques asked in viva: pencil/fountain-pen and potato-peeler (seminar p10)
Curette removes soft lesional tissue preferentially; normal dermis resists

name: Scoop
description: Double-ended instrument with shallow oval spoons, used to scoop out cavity contents and granulation tissue.
parts: Oval, spoon-shaped shallow pointed expansion at either end
types: Small, medium and large sizes; small to medium most used
uses: Scooping out contents of cysts, abscesses and ulcers
Removal of hyperplastic granulation tissue around an ingrown toenail
Ulcer debridement, corn enucleation (seminar)
Nail surgery; applying cell pellet in cell-based vitiligo surgery (PPT1)
how_to_hold: Pencil (fountain-pen) grip between thumb, index and middle finger, or potato-peeler grip with the handle in the distal interdigital fold of the index finger and thumb as a stable base; stretch the skin with the other hand.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Larger and deeper than a molluscum curette
Considered a modification of the curette (PPT1)

name: Hypodermic needle
description: Disposable hollow needle that doubles in dermatology as an extractor, cutting tool, hook and injection device.
uses: Intramuscular, intravenous, subcutaneous injections
Intralesional injection: corticosteroid, 5-fluorouracil, bleomycin, interferon, sodium stibogluconate
Intramatricial steroid injection in nail psoriasis and nail lichen planus
Infiltration anaesthesia before procedures
Aspiration/drainage of bullae (e.g. bullous pemphigoid), vesicles, seroma or haematoma under grafts
Extraction of milia (rice-grain contents also confirm diagnosis), comedones, molluscum
Puncturing closed comedones before extraction
Distinguishing a papule from a small vesicle
Ear and nose piercing
Chemical cauterisation of sebaceous cyst / steatocystoma (Khopkar) and xanthelasma (seminar)
Subcision of acne scars
Intradermal tests: prick, Mantoux, pathergy, Kveim, Frei, Ito-Reenstierna, Montenegro, histamine/pilocarpine, ASST
Needling in vitiligo and molluscum
Drainage of paronychial or small abscess, acne pustule
Slit making in hair transplantation; transferring mini-punch grafts in vitiligo
Intralesional cryotherapy, FNAC
As a hook: nerve biopsy, knot opening, suture cutting
how_to_hold: Mounted on a syringe for injections; used bare (or bent tip) as a lancet, extractor or hook.
sterilization: Commercially pre-packed and sterilised by gamma irradiation; single use.
tips: Khopkar lists chemical cauterisation of sebaceous cyst/steatocystoma; the seminar lists xanthelasma
Classify uses as needle as extractor / cutting instrument / hook / injecting device for viva

name: Skin biopsy punch
description: Cylindrical circular blade on a handle that cuts a full-thickness core of skin.
parts: Cylindrical shaft with sharp circular cutting tip
Stylet with guard in metal punches (gauges graft depth and protects the tip)
types: Metal reusable punches - tapering or cylindrical tips; some with interchangeable tips on one handle
uses: Diagnostic, therapeutic and prognostic skin biopsy
Excisional biopsy of small naevus, solitary molluscum, pyogenic granuloma, digitate wart
Punch grafting in localised stable vitiligo
Lipoma excision by narrow-hole extrusion technique
Hair transplantation
Acne scar surgery: punch excision, punch elevation, punch grafting
Punch excision of small tattoos and melanocytic naevi
Nail matrix/nail bed biopsy (PPT1)
how_to_hold: Held vertically between thumb and index finger like a pencil, perpendicular to the skin.
method: Stretch skin perpendicular to the relaxed skin tension lines
Press and rotate the punch in one direction until the subcutis is reached
Lift the core gently (skin hook/needle), cut the base with scissors
Close with suture or let heal by secondary intention
sterilization: Metal punches: autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde, boiling. Disposable plastic punches: 2% glutaraldehyde.
tips: Remove the stylet before biopsy and flush the hollow during cleaning
Up to 3 mm punches are used on the face for cosmetic reasons
3.5 or 4 mm is the usual diagnostic size (PPT1)

name: Power punch
description: Punch shaft mounted on a motorised handpiece that rotates it at set speed.
parts: Punch shaft with circular cutting edge
uses: Same as hand punches
Follicular unit extraction (FUE) in hair transplantation
Rapid harvesting of multiple punch grafts
method: Mount punch on handpiece
Set rotational speed (2000-10,000 rpm per Khopkar)
Apply perpendicular to skin to required depth
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Speed is adjustable, giving faster and more uniform cuts than manual punches

name: Chalazion clamp
description: Screw-tightened ring clamp that isolates and compresses tissue to give a bloodless field.
parts: Two arms joined at one end, free at the other
Screw to approximate the arms and hold them in position
Free ends expanded: one a flat plate, the other a ring/perforated plate with a large flat thin rim
uses: Mucocele excision / deroofing
Haemostasis during excision of lip pyogenic granuloma or other neoplasm
Reducing bleeding during tongue biopsy
Ear lobe surgery and repair
Oral mucosal and minor salivary gland biopsy; scrotal surgery; lesions on ala nasi (PPT1)
how_to_hold: Place ring over the lesion, plate on the opposite side, tighten screw; the clamp then holds itself.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Originally an eyelid (chalazion) instrument; dermatologists use it on lip, tongue, ear lobe

name: Bard-Parker handle
description: Flat reusable handle onto whose grooved tip a disposable surgical blade is mounted to form a scalpel.
parts: Long flat body (often with metric ruler)
Grooved, tapered blunt tip that receives the blade
types: Other handles: No. 7, Siegel (round-bodied, held like a pen), Beaver (PPT1)
uses: Mounting a surgical blade for incision, excision, shave and other procedures
how_to_hold: Pencil grip for fine dermatological incisions; table-knife grip for long firm cuts; violin-bow grip for long light strokes.
method: Attach: hold blade with artery forceps/needle holder, slide its slot onto the grooved tip until it clicks
Remove: lift the blade heel with the forceps and push it off the tip away from you
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Never load or unload blades with fingers
Seminar lists blade 9 also fitting No. 3; Khopkar says 10, 11, 12, 15

name: Surgical blade
description: Disposable steel blade with a slot that fits a Bard-Parker handle; shape and number decide its use.
parts: Belly with one sharp cutting edge
Linear slot that fits the handle groove
types: No. 15 - small, rounded belly (most used in dermatosurgery); 15C/15D finer
uses: No. 11: stab incision, drainage of abscess, shave biopsy
No. 15: slit-skin smear (leprosy, leishmaniasis); incisions on thin skin such as eyelids and face
Nos. 20-24: incision and excision; Tzanck smear; molluscum smear; paring of warts and corns
how_to_hold: As for the scalpel - pencil grip for precision.
sterilization: Commercially pre-sterilised by gamma irradiation (cold sterilisation); single use.
tips: Higher number = larger blade within each handle range
15 is the workhorse blade for skin surgery

name: Humby's knife
description: Hand-held skin-graft knife with an adjustable roller guard for cutting split-thickness grafts.
parts: Adjustable screws to set graft thickness
Roller that flattens the skin ahead of the blade
uses: Harvesting split-thickness skin grafts (e.g. for stable vitiligo, ulcers)
how_to_hold: Held at the handle with the blade nearly flat to stretched, lubricated donor skin; cut with a to-and-fro sawing movement.
method: Set graft thickness by the screws (check the gap against a blade edge)
Lubricate and stretch donor skin with boards
Advance with to-and-fro oscillating strokes, roller leading
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde
tips: Watson modification is the most commonly used (PPT1)

name: Silver's knife
description: Smaller version of Humby's knife that takes a disposable shaving (razor) blade.
parts: Clamp holding an ordinary disposable shaving blade
uses: Harvesting small, thin split-thickness grafts
Grafts from awkward areas (dorsa of hands, face, scalp) where Humby's knife cannot reach
how_to_hold: Like Humby's knife, held flat to the stretched skin with gentle sawing strokes.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde
tips: Cheap: uses ordinary razor blades

name: Dermatome
description: Disposable or powered device that harvests split-thickness skin grafts of set thickness.
types: Simon Davol dermatome - small rechargeable unit for small grafts
Brown (electric) dermatome - adjustable split-thickness graft depth, about 0.2-0.75 mm (0.008-0.030 inch)
uses: Harvesting split-thickness skin grafts
tips: Graft thickness corrected from source (Khopkar prints 3-8 mm) to the standard split-thickness range of about 0.2-0.75 mm

name: Dissecting forceps
description: Non-locking V-shaped spring forceps used to hold tissue during dissection, suturing and dressing.
parts: Two blades/arms fused at one end and free at the other
types: Plain (non-toothed) - transverse serrations, less traumatic; for nerves, biopsy tissue and delicate structures
Toothed - usually 2 teeth on one jaw interlocking with 1 on the other (1x2); firmer grip, more traumatic; for dermis and cyst walls
uses: Holding tissue during dissection, suturing and dressing
Plain: delicate structures, biopsy specimens
Toothed: skin/dermis, cyst wall
how_to_hold: Hold like a pen with the first three fingers (between thumb and middle finger, index finger steadying); grasp dermis rather than epidermis to avoid crushing the wound edge.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Do not crush the epidermis - pick up dermis
Plain = less traumatic; toothed = better grip but more traumatic

name: Adson forceps
description: Small, light thumb forceps with wide ridged handle tapering to a fine tip, used for handling skin.
parts: Broad ridged handle for controlled grip
Tips plain or with small interlocking teeth
uses: Holding skin edges during suturing (relatively atraumatic) - except eyelids
Suture removal
Handling punch grafts
Holding recipient plugs in hair transplant (PPT1)
how_to_hold: Hold like a pen with the first three fingers (between thumb and middle finger, index finger steadying); grasp dermis rather than epidermis to avoid crushing the wound edge.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Workhorse forceps of dermatosurgery

name: Adson-Brown forceps
description: Adson-type forceps whose tips carry two rows of many fine interlocking teeth, for delicate tissue.
parts: Two rows of fine interlocking teeth at the tip
uses: Gentle handling of superficial, delicate tissue and skin edges
how_to_hold: Hold like a pen with the first three fingers (between thumb and middle finger, index finger steadying); grasp dermis rather than epidermis to avoid crushing the wound edge.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Many small teeth spread the grip, so less crush than 1x2 teeth

name: DeBakey forceps
description: Atraumatic thumb forceps with fine longitudinal serrations on the jaws.
parts: One jaw with two parallel rows of serrations, the other with a single central row (longitudinal)
uses: Atraumatic holding of delicate tissue and vessels
how_to_hold: Hold like a pen with the first three fingers (between thumb and middle finger, index finger steadying); grasp dermis rather than epidermis to avoid crushing the wound edge.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Originally a vascular forceps; non-toothed

name: Iris forceps
description: Fine, narrow-bladed forceps with gradually tapering tips for delicate grafting work.
parts: Narrow blades tapering gradually (more gradual than Adson)
Spring forceps - no lock or ratchet
types: Graefe, Stevens, Bishop-Harmon, Foerster, Gill, Tuebingen patterns (PPT1)
Bishop-Harmon: fenestrated handle, fine tips (sometimes 1x2 teeth), horizontal or crisscross serrations (seminar)
uses: Miniature punch grafting
Acne scar surgery
Split-thickness and blister grafting (PPT1)
how_to_hold: Hold like a pen with the first three fingers (between thumb and middle finger, index finger steadying); grasp dermis rather than epidermis to avoid crushing the wound edge.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Corrected from source: Khopkar/PPT2 mention a 'lock'; iris forceps have no lock
Originally an ophthalmic forceps for handling the iris
Bishop-Harmon is grouped here (PPT1 lists it as an iris forceps type; seminar gives a separate slide)

name: Jeweller's forceps
description: Plain-handled forceps that taper rapidly to very fine points, for atraumatic micro-handling.
parts: Rapid taper to a fine tip
uses: Atraumatic handling of skin grafts
Hair transplantation (graft implantation)
Suture removal
Grasping small bleeders during electrocoagulation
how_to_hold: Hold like a pen with the first three fingers (between thumb and middle finger, index finger steadying); grasp dermis rather than epidermis to avoid crushing the wound edge.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

name: Ring forceps
description: Fine forceps like iris forceps but without teeth or serrations, with a curved fine tip.
uses: Hair transplantation
how_to_hold: Hold like a pen with the first three fingers (between thumb and middle finger, index finger steadying); grasp dermis rather than epidermis to avoid crushing the wound edge.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

name: Hair transplant forceps
description: Fine forceps designed to grasp follicular grafts without crushing them, for extraction and implantation.
types: Extraction forceps - fine sharp tips to pull follicles from donor area
Implantation forceps - insert grafts into recipient slits
Jeweller's, Foerster, Castroviejo and Adson hair-transplant patterns
Plain, groove, hex tips; straight or curved (seminar figures)
uses: Follicular unit extraction (FUE)
Follicular unit transplantation (FUT/strip) graft handling and implantation
how_to_hold: Hold like a pen with the first three fingers (between thumb and middle finger, index finger steadying); grasp dermis rather than epidermis to avoid crushing the wound edge.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Hold the graft by the perifollicular tissue, never the bulb
Not a separate Khopkar entry; Khopkar lists ring forceps and jeweller's forceps for hair transplantation (p409)

name: Epilation forceps
description: Small forceps with serrated tips used to pluck hairs and remove sutures.
uses: Epilation
Suture removal
how_to_hold: Hold like a pen with the first three fingers (between thumb and middle finger, index finger steadying); grasp dermis rather than epidermis to avoid crushing the wound edge.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

name: Dressing forceps
description: Long, serrated non-locking forceps used to handle dressings.
parts: Wider, flatter tip than tissue forceps
uses: Holding medicated dressings and gauze during wound care
how_to_hold: Hold like a pen with the first three fingers (between thumb and middle finger, index finger steadying); grasp dermis rather than epidermis to avoid crushing the wound edge.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Khopkar: serrated; seminar: may be smooth or serrated

name: Allis forceps
description: Ring-handled locking forceps with interdigitating teeth for a secure grip on tissue to be removed.
parts: Two straight blades, separated except at the tip
Ratchet lock near the handle (3 catches)
Blades riveted together - the joint acts as fulcrum
uses: Corn enucleation
Cyst excision (holding the cyst/tissue being removed)
how_to_hold: Thumb and ring finger in the rings, index finger along the shanks for control; ratchet engaged/released by pressing the rings together and apart.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Traumatic - hold only tissue that will be removed (PPT1)

name: Cheatle forceps
description: Long L-shaped forceps without teeth or lock, kept in antiseptic to pick up sterile items.
parts: Somewhat L-shaped arms without teeth or lock
Proximal rings for thumb and ring finger (or one ring and a V-bend)
Sinuous distal part with curved serrated jaws
uses: Picking up sterile instruments, gauze and dressing material from trays/drums
how_to_hold: Thumb and ring finger in rings; keep tips pointing down so fluid does not run back onto the handle.
sterilization: Distal part kept immersed in antiseptic (e.g. Savlon) in its jar; autoclave periodically.
tips: Must be stored in a bottle of Savlon / antiseptic
Never touch the patient with it

name: Artery forceps
description: Ring-handled locking clamp with blunt serrated tapering jaws used to catch bleeders and grasp tissue.
parts: Blunt tapering jaws with transverse serrations
types: Kelly - 5-7 inch, serrations on distal part of jaw only
Crile / Rochester-Pean - largest, serrations along entire jaw
uses: Catching bleeding vessels
Holding the free end of a suture
Blunt dissection of lipoma and cysts
Crushing the pedicle of pedunculated lesions (acrochordon, DPN)
Removing nail plate in partial nail avulsion
Three-point traction during circumcision
Plucking hairs for trichogram
how_to_hold: Thumb and ring finger in the rings, index finger along the shanks for control; ratchet engaged/released by pressing the rings together and apart.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Size order: Mosquito < Kelly < Crile/Pean
Medium and small sizes are most used in dermatosurgery (PPT1)

name: Sponge holding forceps
description: Long ring-handled locking forceps with fenestrated oval jaws for holding gauze swabs.
parts: Long shanks with ring handles and ratchet
Transverse serrations on inner jaw surface
uses: Holding cotton/gauze swabs to paint the operative site with antiseptic before surgery
how_to_hold: Thumb and ring finger in the rings, index finger along the shanks for control; ratchet engaged/released by pressing the rings together and apart.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

name: Towel clip
description: Small ring-handled locking clip with curved pointed tips that fixes drapes in place.
parts: Curved sharp or blunt tips that meet
uses: Securing surgical drapes and towels so they do not slip during a procedure
how_to_hold: Thumb and ring finger in the rings, index finger along the shanks for control; ratchet engaged/released by pressing the rings together and apart.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

name: Needle holder
description: Ring-handled locking instrument with short strong jaws that grips the suture needle.
parts: Short jaws, smooth or serrated, with a central groove
Ratchet lock (Khopkar: in the proximal part)
types: Crile-Wood - finer, rounded tip for delicate needles
Ryder - small, fine tips for 4-0/5-0 needles (PPT1)
uses: Grasping and driving the needle during suturing
Instrument tying of knots
how_to_hold: Finger (ring) grip with thumb and ring finger in rings and index finger on the shank, or palm (thenar) grip with rings in the palm for speed. Grasp the needle at the junction of its middle and posterior thirds (2/3:1/3 rule), near the jaw tip.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Do not grip the swaged end - it bends/breaks
Khopkar places the lock proximally; the seminar says near the jaws - follow Khopkar

name: Castroviejo needle holder
description: Small spring-handled needle holder with a lock, for fine needles in delicate surgery.
uses: Fine suturing with 6-0 and smaller sutures
Delicate surgery such as mini hair grafts and acne scar revision (Khopkar)
how_to_hold: Held like a pencil between thumb and index/middle fingers; spring action opens and closes the jaws.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

name: Suturing needle
description: Curved or straight needle that carries suture through tissue; classified by curvature and cross-section.
types: Shank: closed eye (suture threaded) or swaged (suture attached)
Conventional cutting - third edge on inner curve
Reverse cutting - third edge on outer curve; preferred for skin under tension
Round-bodied - no cutting edge; mucosa, subcutaneous sutures
uses: Suturing skin, mucosa and subcutaneous tissue
how_to_hold: Held in a needle holder at the junction of middle and posterior thirds.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde, boiling (swaged suture-needles come gamma-sterilised).
tips: Conventional cutting needles tend to cut through the wound margin; reverse cutting avoids this

name: Suture materials
description: Threads used to close wounds, graded from 11-0 (finest) to 3 (thickest).
types: Absorbable: catgut, polyglycolic acid (Dexon), polyglactin 910 (Vicryl), polydioxanone (PDS), poliglecaprone (Monocryl)
Non-absorbable: silk, nylon (Ethilon), polyester (Mersilene), polypropylene (Prolene), polybutester
Multifilament: silk, cotton, linen, braided nylon, polyglactin
uses: 3-0/4-0: scalp, back, extremities, facial wounds under tension
5-0: face, scrotum
6-0: eyelids
Most dermatosurgery uses 3-0 to 6-0
sterilization: Gamma irradiation (factory pre-sterilised).
tips: Sizes thicker than 1-0 carry the '#' prefix
Other closure aids: cyanoacrylate glue, fibrin glue, closure tapes (Steri-Strip), staples; tincture benzoin as tactifier

name: Iris scissors
description: Small, sharp-pointed scissors with a long rivet-to-tip distance and short shank for fine dissection.
parts: Two blades pivoting on a rivet/screw that acts as fulcrum; ring handles
One blade may be serrated for tissue grip
uses: Fine dissection in dermatosurgery
Serrated variant for thin skin
Cutting delicate tissue and mucous membranes, skin biopsy, enucleation of cyst/lipoma (PPT1)
how_to_hold: Tripod grip: thumb and ring finger in the rings (only up to the distal phalanx), index finger resting near the screw joint for stability.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Originally ophthalmic; do not use for cutting sutures or dressings - blunts the tips

name: Castroviejo scissors
description: Delicate spring-handled micro-scissors with small cutting tips.
uses: Surgery on mucosa and thin-skinned areas such as eyelids
Harvesting suction blister grafts
Cutting thin split-thickness / blister grafts (PPT1)
how_to_hold: Held like a pencil; squeeze the spring handles to cut.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

name: Dressing scissors
description: Straight scissors with one thick blunt blade and one sharp blade, for cutting dressings and sutures.
parts: Two blades pivoting on a rivet/screw that acts as fulcrum; ring handles
Lower blade thick and blunt (slides under the dressing, protects skin)
Upper blade sharp - cuts as the scissors close
uses: Cutting dressings and bandages without injuring skin
Cutting sutures
how_to_hold: Tripod grip: thumb and ring finger in the rings (only up to the distal phalanx), index finger resting near the screw joint for stability.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

name: Curved scissors
description: Sharp scissors with curved blades that give better reach and visibility in deeper dissection.
parts: Two blades pivoting on a rivet/screw that acts as fulcrum; ring handles
uses: Cutting tissue
Negotiating difficult-to-reach areas during deeper dissection
how_to_hold: Tripod grip: thumb and ring finger in the rings (only up to the distal phalanx), index finger resting near the screw joint for stability.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Straight scissors give mechanical advantage for tough tissue; curved give more directional mobility and visibility (seminar)

name: Undermining scissors
description: Longer scissors with blunt, broad tips for undermining and blunt dissection with minimal trauma.
parts: Two blades pivoting on a rivet/screw that acts as fulcrum; ring handles
uses: Undermining wound edges before closure
Soft tissue and blunt dissection
how_to_hold: Tripod grip: thumb and ring finger in the rings (only up to the distal phalanx), index finger resting near the screw joint for stability.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

name: Mayo scissors
description: Heavy, robust scissors for cutting thick tissue such as fascia and cartilage.
parts: Two blades pivoting on a rivet/screw that acts as fulcrum; ring handles
Short heavy blades, sturdier than Metzenbaum
uses: Cutting thick tissue (fascia, cartilage)
Straight Mayo commonly used to cut sutures in general surgery
how_to_hold: Tripod grip: thumb and ring finger in the rings (only up to the distal phalanx), index finger resting near the screw joint for stability.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Mayo = short handle, heavy blades; Metzenbaum = long handle, fine blades

name: Suture removal scissors
description: Small scissors with a hooked or notched lower blade that slips under a stitch to cut it.
parts: Two blades pivoting on a rivet/screw that acts as fulcrum; ring handles
Small hook / concavity on one blade
uses: Safe, quick removal of sutures
how_to_hold: Tripod grip: thumb and ring finger in the rings (only up to the distal phalanx), index finger resting near the screw joint for stability.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Specialised (fine) scissors should not be used for cutting sutures - use these instead

name: Skin hook
description: Handle ending in one or more fine hooks that lift skin edges with less trauma than forceps.
uses: Holding skin margins during suturing, especially thin skin (eyelids)
Retracting skin margins during deeper dissection and undermining
Holding vital structures such as nerves during procedures/biopsy
Rakes for retracting large wound areas
Repair of dog-ears; everting wound edges while undermining (seminar)
how_to_hold: Held like a pencil; hook inserted into the dermis of the wound edge and lifted gently.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Preferred to forceps because they do not crush tissue
Sharp hooks can injure the operator - handle carefully

name: Liposuction cannula
description: Hollow blunt metal tube with side openings at the tip, attached to syringe or suction to remove fat.
parts: Distal tip with one or more openings where fat enters
Proximal end that attaches to syringe or suction device
types: Short cannulas for face; long for back and outer thigh
uses: Liposuction / fat harvesting (e.g. for fat grafting)
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Large cannula: more dead cells, more complications; small cannula: better fat take (seminar figure)

name: Loupes
description: Binocular magnifying devices (about 2-4x) worn during examination and surgery.
uses: Better visualisation for suturing and spotting bleeding points
Biopsy, excision, hair transplant and reconstructive surgery
Better posture and less eye strain in long procedures

name: Nail nipper / nail splitter
description: Stout plier-like cutter used to cut the nail plate in nail surgery.
parts: Strong blades with sharp cutting edges
Splitter: one wedge-shaped blunt (anvil) blade and one sharp cutting blade
uses: Cutting the nail plate during partial nail avulsion
how_to_hold: Held in the palm like pliers; in a splitter the blunt anvil blade goes under the nail plate.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Khopkar distinguishes nipper (both edges sharp) from splitter (anvil + sharp); seminar/PPT treat them as one

name: Nail spatula
description: Double-ended instrument with flat curved plates used to separate the nail plate from surrounding tissue.
parts: Flat, rectangular, curved plates at either end
uses: Separating nail plate from nail bed
Separating proximal nail fold from nail plate
Lifting dressing from skin or punch grafts
how_to_hold: Pencil grip; advance the plate under the nail with gentle to-and-fro movements.
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

name: Manual dermabrader
description: Hand-held abrader with a toothed, slightly curved rectangular tip, devised by Dr Rustom Maneksha.
parts: Handle with or without thumb rest
Sharp teeth in regular rows and columns on the convex surface
uses: Vitiligo: abrading recipient area for suction blister or split-thickness grafts; stimulating melanocyte proliferation and migration
Lichen amyloidosis, lichen simplex chronicus
Spot dermabrasion of acne scars
Full-face dermabrasion for rejuvenation
Debulking rhinophyma
Multiple adenoma sebaceum
Tattoo removal
Freshening edges in ear lobe repair
how_to_hold: Gripped with four fingers around the handle and thumb on the thumb rest; skin stretched with the other hand.
method: Stretch and anaesthetise the area
Abrade with firm back-and-forth strokes
End point: pin-point bleeding (papillary dermis)
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Indian innovation - Maneksha's dermabrader is a favourite viva spot

name: Motorised dermabrader
description: Motor-driven handpiece that spins diamond fraises or wire brushes to abrade skin at controlled speed.
parts: Motor / control unit with foot pedal
Attachments: diamond fraise or wire brush
types: Diamond fraises - diamond chips bonded to steel wheels; regular, coarse, extra-coarse (coarser = deeper)
Wire brushes - short steel wires; abrade deeper than fraises
Burrs of various shapes (ball, pear, cylinder, cone, wheel)
uses: Same indications as manual dermabrasion (vitiligo recipient site, scars, rhinophyma, amyloidosis)
Driving FUE punches in hair transplant
Bone/nail burring (osteophyte removal) - seminar
method: Choose fraise/brush by depth needed
Set speed; depth depends on burr type, speed, pressure, duration and skin condition
sterilization: Fraises/brushes: autoclave; handpiece per manufacturer
tips: Speed: Khopkar 3000-30,000 rpm (seminar text garbled as '3,000 and 0,000 rpm')
Wire brush abrades deeper than diamond fraise

name: Skin graft spreader
description: Straight metal rod of uniform diameter with blunt ends used to spread thin grafts.
uses: Spreading suction blister or split-thickness grafts over the recipient area
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

name: Suction blister apparatus
description: Suction machine or syringe assembly that raises epidermal blisters for epidermal grafting in vitiligo.
parts: Suction machine: suction pump, vacuum gauge, glass cup with non-traumatic rim
Syringe technique: 20/50/100 ml disposable syringes with pistons removed, three-way cannula (Disofix), 50-100 ml syringe for negative pressure
uses: Raising suction blisters for epidermal (blister-roof) grafting in stable vitiligo
method: Clean donor site (anterolateral thigh, flexor forearm, abdomen); shave hair
Interconnect syringes via three-way cannulas, open ends on skin
Withdraw piston of the end syringe to create negative pressure; close the three-way
Blister forms in 1-2 h from dermo-epidermal separation
sterilization: Glass cups must be sterilised; syringes are disposable.
tips: Syringe method: cheap, less painful, no sterilisation, easy
Blister grafts: good colour match, no pebbling; suitable for eyelids, lips, glans
Machine: expensive, bulky, needs special cups

name: Semmes-Weinstein monofilament
description: Colour-coded nylon filaments that bend at a fixed force, used to test protective touch sensation.
types: Red 4 g - loss of protective sensation
uses: Screening for sensory neuropathy
Measuring sensory loss in leprosy, diabetes and other neuropathies
Detecting silent neuritis in leprosy (test every 2 weeks for 4 months, then monthly)
how_to_hold: Hold perpendicular to the skin and press until the filament bends into a 'C'.
method: Test hands at 7 sites (3 ulnar, 3 median, 1 radial)
Test feet at the standard 10 sites: plantar 1st, 3rd and 5th metatarsal heads; plantar distal hallux, 3rd and 5th toes; medial and lateral midfoot; heel; dorsum between 1st and 2nd toes
Ask the patient (eyes closed) if felt
Failure at any tested point = positive
tips: Designed by Josephine Semmes and Sidney Weinstein
Inability to feel the purple filament = loss of protective sensation
Foot test sites corrected from source to the standard 10-site examination

name: Sim's anterior vaginal wall retractor
description: Long thin instrument with angled, serrated oval fenestrated ends that lifts the anterior vaginal wall.
parts: Expanded oval fenestrated loops at both ends, angled to the shaft (about 15 degrees, facing opposite directions)
Serrations on the loops for grip
uses: Used with Sim's speculum during gynaecological examination and procedures
Retracting anterior vaginal wall to see cervix and fornices
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

name: Sim's speculum
description: Double-ended curved-plate vaginal speculum that depresses the posterior wall.
parts: Two curved blades (plates) of different sizes
Trough / central depression along the length
uses: Visualising anterior and lateral vaginal walls, fornices, cervix and os
Differentiating cervical from vaginal discharge
Seeing strawberry cervix (trichomoniasis)
Collecting discharge: wet mount (Trichomonas), KOH/Gram (Candida), clue cells (Gardnerella)
Pap smear
Treating cervical/vaginal warts (podophyllin, cryotherapy)
Acetowhitening test with 3-5% acetic acid
method: Warm in water before use
Patient in left lateral (Sims) position
Insert one blade vertically, then rotate 90 degrees to depress posterior wall
Lift anterior wall with Sim's retractor; discharge pools in the central trough
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Disadvantages: patient brought to table edge; clinician's hands are not free (needs assistant/retractor)

name: Cusco's self-retaining vaginal speculum
description: Bivalve speculum resembling a bird's beak that is locked open by a screw, freeing the examiner's hands.
parts: Two blades, concave inside with rounded free margins, riveted together
Handles at right angles to blades
Screw lock to hold blades apart
types: Small for nulliparous, large for multiparous/prolapse
uses: Visualising cervix
Pap smear, cervical biopsy, swab collection
Chemical cauterisation / cryotherapy of cervical warts
IUCD insertion, colposcopy (seminar)
method: Insert with blades closed (Khopkar: oriented vertically)
After full insertion rotate 90 degrees (Khopkar: anticlockwise) so handle points down
Press handles to open blades and tighten the screw
Before removal loosen the screw, close the blades and withdraw
sterilization: Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling
tips: Self-retaining: hands free for procedures; patient need not move to table edge
Disadvantage: anterior and posterior walls are hidden by the blades
Seminar wording: enter at 9 o'clock then rotate to 6/12 o'clock - follow Khopkar's description
Seminar/PPT: preferred in cryosurgery as it shields the vaginal walls; not ideal for vaginal surgery

name: Wood's lamp
description: Hand-held long-wave UVA source whose induced fluorescence helps diagnose skin, hair and systemic conditions.
parts: Wood's filter (barium silicate with 9% nickel oxide)
Many models: white light and magnifying lens
AC power supply; output <1 mW/cm2; peak 365 nm (320-400 nm)
uses: Pityriasis versicolor - golden yellow
Tinea capitis: M. canis, M. audouinii, M. distortum, M. ferrugineum - blue-green; M. gypseum - dull yellow; T. schoenleinii - dull blue
Pseudomonas - greenish (pyoverdin); erythrasma - coral red (coproporphyrin III)
Vitiligo - chalky/bright blue-white; nevus depigmentosus vs nevus anemicus
Typing melasma (epidermal accentuates)
Porphyrias - pink fluorescence of urine, teeth, tears etc.; acne - orange-red (P. acnes porphyrins)
Scabies burrows (tetracycline/fluorescein)
Checking even application of peel or barrier cream
Therapeutic: vitiligo when UV source unavailable (long exposures)
Non-dermatological: forged currency/signatures, semen detection, cracks in metal
how_to_hold: Held 4-5 inches (10-13 cm) from the skin in a dark room.
method: Darken the room (or use a hood)
Pre-warm the lamp for about 1 minute
Hold 4-5 inches from the lesion
Examine before the patient washes the area
tips: Invented by physicist Robert W. Wood (1903)
False negative: washing removes water-soluble coproporphyrin in erythrasma
False positive: white coat (light blue), scales, salicylic ointment (green), petrolatum (bluish-purple)

name: Dermoscope
description: Hand-held illuminated magnifier that shows subsurface skin structures not visible to the naked eye.
types: With image capture (e.g. Dermlite Foto, Delta 20, Video episcope)
With capture and analysis (e.g. MoleMax, FotoFinder)
Contact (glass plate + linkage fluid) vs non-contact polarised
uses: Pigmented lesions - naevi, early melanoma
Psoriasis, lichen planus, dermatofibroma, Darier's disease, cicatricial alopecia, seborrhoeic keratosis, urticarial vasculitis
Follicular density of donor area before hair transplant
Nail-fold capillaroscopy (small plates)
method: Contact: apply linkage fluid, place glass plate on lesion
Non-contact: cross-polarised lens held just above skin
sterilization: Contact plates: 2% glutaraldehyde, methylated spirit, boiling or autoclaving.
tips: Non-contact avoids cross-infection but gives less illumination and resolution

name: Electrocautery / electrosurgical unit
description: Device converting mains current into high-frequency oscillating current that destroys, coagulates or cuts tissue.
parts: Electrode probes - pointed, bent, straight, blade, ball, wire, Teflon-coated, forceps electrode
types: Spark gap - damped wave: fulguration, desiccation, coagulation (most used in India)
Solid state - all/blended waves: coagulation and cutting
Electrofulguration (no touch, 1-3 mm gap; power 1-2): verruca plana, DPN, milia
Electrodesiccation (touch; power 5-7): SK, warts, pyogenic granuloma, acrochordon, xanthelasma, superficial BCC
Electrocoagulation (power 7-10, ground plate): telangiectasia, BCC, nail matrix ablation, bleeders
Electrosection (cutting, 5-10 mm/s): keloid, acne keloidalis, rhinophyma
uses: Destruction of benign/superficial lesions
Haemostasis
Cutting (electrosection)
method: Clean electrode with blade/sand paper or wet gauze
Choose mode and power
Do not forcibly pull off eschar
sterilization: Probes are self-sterilising from heat; disposable electrodes may be preferred.
tips: Keep alcohol/ether away; let spirit evaporate fully
Use smoke evacuator within 2 cm or mask (HPV, HBV, HIV in plume)
Avoid infiltrating anaesthetic over telangiectasia (blanches vessels)
William Bovie - father of modern electrosurgery

name: Electrolysis (galvanic) epilator
description: Direct-current device that generates caustic sodium hydroxide in the follicle to destroy the hair bulb.
parts: Dispersive electrode on anode (positive) held against skin
uses: Permanent hair removal (electroepilation)
method: Insert cathode needle into the hair follicle
Patient holds/contacts the anode
Current ionises tissue water and salt: NaOH forms at cathode and destroys the bulb
tips: Products: NaOH (lye) and H2 at cathode; HCl and Cl2 at anode

name: Radiofrequency surgical unit
description: Electrosurgery at very high frequency (500-4000 kHz) giving precise cutting/coagulation with little lateral heat damage.
types: Cut mode (pure wave): skin tags, naevi, cysts, shave of xanthelasma, verruca plana
Cut-and-coagulate (blended): curettage, SK, keloids, warts, BCC, Bowen's, SCC, Paget's, debulking rhinophyma, large pyogenic granuloma
Coagulation mode: pyogenic granuloma, haemangioma, telangiectasia
uses: Same as electrocautery, with choice of mode
tips: Advantages: less lateral spread, better scars, less infection, easier bleeding control
Disadvantages: expensive, fragile costly probes

name: Cryotherapy unit
description: Liquid-nitrogen container with spray tips and probes used to freeze and destroy lesions.
parts: Insulated canister for liquid nitrogen with trigger valve
Spray tips / cones / cylinders (open and closed methods)
Accessories: eye protection (Jaeger retractor, goggles), cotton plugs, tongue depressor, thermocouple needles, chamois bag for CO2
types: Cryospray - open (spot, paintbrush, spiral, rotatory) and closed (cones)
Cryoroller - metal roller dipped in LN2 (acne scars, keloids)
Intralesional cryo through spinal needle (thick keloids)
Cryoslush - solid CO2 with acetone (acne, scars)
uses: Benign: warts, molluscum, keloid, hypertrophic scar, pyogenic granuloma, skin tags, SK, mucous/myxoid cyst, angioma
Premalignant: leukoplakia, Bowen's, actinic keratosis, erythroplasia of Queyrat
Malignant: BCC (not morphoeic), SCC, LMM, palliation
Softening keloid before intralesional steroid
Cooling during laser; frozen section; topical anaesthesia (ethyl chloride); cutaneous myiasis
contraindications: Cold intolerance, Raynaud's, cryoglobulinaemia, cold urticaria
method: Fill unit with LN2 to 2 inches below brim; wait 3-4 min for pressure
Mark lesion margin; spray at centre from about 1 cm
Let ice ball thaw completely before 2nd freeze-thaw cycle
Probe size about 3/4 of lesion size; remove probe only after thawing
sterilization: Accessories: dry heat, autoclave or 2% glutaraldehyde.
tips: Liquid nitrogen -196 C (spray), about -20 C on swab
Melanocytes die at -4 to -8 C, so hypopigmentation is common
Thaw time is about twice freeze time; fast freeze, slow thaw kills best
James Arnott - father of cryosurgery

name: Lasers
aka: LASER - Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation
description: Devices emitting coherent, collimated, monochromatic light that selectively destroys target chromophores.
parts: Optical resonator - 100% and partially reflecting mirrors
Power/pumping source (electrical, flash lamp, chemical, diode)
uses: Hair reduction: long-pulsed Nd:YAG 1064 (dark skin), diode 800, alexandrite 755, IPL
Pigment and tattoos: Q-switched Nd:YAG 1064/532, ruby 694, alexandrite 755
Vascular: PDL 585 nm, alexandrite, Nd:YAG, argon-pumped dye, krypton, copper vapour
Ablative resurfacing: CO2 10,600 nm, Er:YAG 2940 nm
Psoriasis/vitiligo: excimer 308 nm
Acne, scars, keloids, warts
tips: Mechanism: selective photothermolysis; photothermal, photomechanical, photoacoustic effects
Know terms: fluence (J/cm2), irradiance, pulse duration, thermal relaxation time, spot size
Precautions: no combustibles, goggles for all, plume evacuator, no reflective instruments

name: Intense pulsed light (IPL)
description: Non-laser xenon flash-lamp source emitting broad-spectrum light (500-1200 nm) that is filtered for the target.
uses: Hair reduction
Non-ablative rejuvenation
Hyperpigmentation (mixed type)
tips: Not a laser: non-coherent, polychromatic; filters let one machine do many tasks

name: Blue and red light devices
description: LED light sources (blue about 400 nm, red 660 nm) that photoactivate porphyrins in acne and photodynamic therapy.
types: Blue light - peak about 400 nm (Soret band)
Red light - 660 nm LED, deeper penetration
uses: Inflammatory and non-inflammatory acne
Photodynamic therapy (with 5-ALA)
tips: P. acnes porphyrins are photo-excited and kill the bacteria

name: Iontophoresis unit
description: Galvanic device that drives charged drug ions or tap-water ions into skin with direct current.
parts: DC source with current control (0-3.8 mA)
uses: Palmoplantar hyperhidrosis
Drug delivery: tretinoin (scars), glycolic acid, retinoids for melasma, sodium salicylate (warts), zinc oxide (ulcer), iodide (scars), idoxuridine (herpes labialis)
Patch testing, pilocarpine (sweat) test
method: Clean area with spirit
Place the drug under the electrode of the same charge: positively charged drug under the anode, negatively charged drug under the cathode; the other electrode is the indifferent one
Tap-water iontophoresis for hyperhidrosis: both palms/soles in water trays, one on each electrode, with polarity reversed midway through the session
Raise current slowly 0-3.8 mA with continuous circular/stroking movement of the electrode; full face takes about 20-25 min
End point mild erythema; reduce to zero and reverse polarity briefly
tips: Principle: like charges repel - cations are driven into skin from the anode, anions from the cathode (corrected from source: Khopkar's acidic-agent/cathode wording dropped)
Grease abrasions; stop and reverse current if pain/burning
Complications: erythema, urticaria, burns, irritant/allergic dermatitis

name: Patch test kit
description: Allergen series and occlusive chambers used to demonstrate type IV contact allergy.
parts: Allergens in petrolatum or other vehicles
Chambers: Al-test discs, Finn chambers (8 mm aluminium), plastic chambers
types: Indian standard series (CODFI) plus cosmetic and footwear series
uses: Confirming allergic contact dermatitis
Photopatch testing for photoallergy
method: Apply to upper back (or outer arm/thigh)
Keep dry for 48 h; remove at 48 h
First reading about 30 min after removal; late readings 48-72 h later and at day 4-7 (ICDRG grading)
tips: Stop systemic steroids (>20 mg/day) and immunosuppressants before testing
Plastic Finn chambers for metals (nickel, cobalt, mercury)
Jadassohn - father of patch testing (1895)
False positives: angry back, irritants, excess concentration

name: Prick test kit
description: Kit of allergen solutions, lancets and stencil used to demonstrate type I (immediate) hypersensitivity.
parts: Allergen solutions in small dropper bottles
uses: Diagnosis of respiratory allergy, chronic urticaria and other IgE-mediated allergy
method: Place allergen drops about 1 inch apart on flexor forearm or back (back preferred in children)
Prick superficially through each drop without drawing blood; wipe lancet between pricks
Read at 20 minutes against controls with the stencil
tips: Stop antihistamines, steroids, mast-cell stabilisers beforehand
Emergency kit (hydrocortisone, adrenaline, chlorpheniramine, bronchodilator) must be ready

name: Common pin
description: Ordinary pin whose head, tip and shaft each serve as simple bedside diagnostic tools.
uses: Head: crude touch sensation in leprosy and neurological conditions
Head: eliciting deep dermal tenderness
Head: showing the feeding vessel of a spider angioma

Head: demonstrating scales - scratch sign (pityriasis versicolor), carpet-tack / cat's-tongue sign (DLE, pemphigus foliaceus), Auspitz sign (psoriasis), wafer-like scale (pityriasis lichenoides chronica)
Head: stroking skin for dermographism and Darier's sign
Head: chemical cauterisation
Tip: pain sensation in leprosy, HSAN, congenital insensitivity to pain
Tip: extracting mites
Shaft: lifting the buried distal end of an ingrowing hair in pseudofolliculitis
tips: Use a fresh sterile pin for each patient when breaking skin

name: Glass slide
description: Plain microscope slide used for diascopy and for preparing smears and mounts.
uses: Diascopy (vitropression): purpura vs erythema; nevus depigmentosus vs nevus anemicus; apple-jelly nodules in lupus vulgaris, sarcoidosis
Therapeutic diascopy: blanching the superficial part of a vascular malformation so laser reaches the deeper part
Testing compressibility of vascular malformations
Smears: imprint, tissue, crush, slit-skin smear for Gram, AFB, Giemsa/Wright stain; KOH (10-20%) mount
Tzanck smear in calcinosis cutis (irregular deep blue basophilic granules)
Elastosis perforans serpiginosa - elastic fibres in keratotic plug (KOH and stain)
Transferring suction blister grafts from donor to recipient site
Preparing hair mounts
method: Diascopy: press the slide firmly on the lesion and look for blanching or residual colour

name: Magnifying lens
description: Hand lens (2x-7x), with or without its own light, for studying fine surface details of lesions.
uses: Studying fine morphology of skin lesions
Nits and lice (pediculosis capitis, pubic lice); lice in clothing seams (pediculosis corporis)
Scabies burrows and mites
Auspitz sign, nail pits, Wickham's striae (lichen planus vs lichenoid drug rash)
Black dots in warts and black-dot tinea capitis
Umbilication in molluscum, penicilliosis
Carpet-tack sign in DLE, seborrhoeic keratosis, Darier's disease, pemphigus foliaceus
Nail-fold telangiectasia in collagen vascular disease
Furrow in the ridged margin of porokeratosis
Exclamation-mark hairs in alopecia areata
Can act as a diascope when no glass slide is available

name: Measuring tape
description: Flexible tape used to measure lesions and body dimensions for documentation and follow-up.
uses: Size of ulcers, plaques, lymph nodes for description and monitoring
Limb hypertrophy (Klippel-Trenaunay, lymphoedema), muscle atrophy (leprosy, hereditary motor neuropathy), limb girth in mycetoma
Induration after Mantoux and other intradermal tests
Chest expansion in scleroderma
Hip/waist ratio in lipodystrophy
Upper:lower segment ratio and arm span in Marfan syndrome

name: Filter paper
description: Absorbent paper used for simple bedside tests and for collecting and preserving specimens.
uses: Checking dapsone adherence in leprosy - urine drop on filter paper dipped in Ehrlich's reagent
Sweat tests: ninhydrin (pink) and bromophenol blue (blue) in leprosy and other neuropathies (diabetes, alcohol, HSAN, porphyria)
Patch testing liquid allergens (formaldehyde, propylene glycol)
Documenting Auspitz sign
Collecting and keeping hair, skin scrapings and nail clippings
Wrapping tattoo pigments for autoclaving

name: Cotton swab stick
description: Wooden stick with a cotton tip used to collect specimens, apply agents and perform simple procedures.
parts: Wooden stick (ear buds or ready-made sterile plastic swabs as alternatives)
uses: Cotton tip: smears and culture swabs of discharges
Applying peels (glycolic acid, TCA, phenol, salicylic acid)
Chemical cauterisation (TCA, phenol)
Cryotherapy by dipstick method
Applying podophyllin to genital warts; acetowhitening for subclinical warts
Cervical swabs; specimens for PCR
Haemostasis in hair transplantation
Spreading ointment on suture lines; applying topical lotions (e.g. psoralen in vitiligo)
Nikolsky sign on mucosa
Stick end: chemical cauterisation of small lesions (DPN, filiform wart, verruca plana, molluscum)
Stick: extraction of guinea worm
sterilization: Autoclave; ready-made swabs for specimen collection are gamma-irradiated.
